strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: negative prompt guidance in few-step distilled diffusion/flow-matching models, where standard CFG fails.

The proposed mechanism (sign-flipping negative prompt values in attention) is simple, single-pass, and computationally efficient; the MMDiT masking/duplication design is thoughtful and well-motivated.

Comprehensive experimental treatment: quantitative MLLM-judge results with significance testing, qualitative comparisons, hyperparameter trade-off curves across all methods, an ablation study (masking, bias, duplication, whole-embedding-flip alternative), attention-map visualizations, computational cost measurements, and adaptation to a video model (Wan 2.1 + CausVid).
Reasonably fair treatment of baselines, including re-tuned NAG (NAG++) and external systems (GPT-4o, Janus-4o, Qwen-Image, generate-then-edit).
Honest reporting of limitations (MLLM judge unreliability, over-removal of features, failure on Flux Schnell).
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea sits incrementally on top of NASA (attention-space negative guidance) and Koulischer et al.'s dynamic guidance; VSF is essentially a token/region-adaptive version of NASA's fixed subtraction realized by sign-flipping values. The contribution is more engineering than conceptual advance.

Evaluation reliability is a major concern. The primary metric is a single MLLM judge (Llama-4 Maverick), which the authors themselves show is unreliable (generous quality scores, hallucinations); a human evaluation is claimed but no results are reported anywhere. Quality/positive scores rely entirely on the same fallible judge.

The evaluation dataset is small (200 GPT-o3-generated prompts, 2 seeds) and prompts/hyperparameters were developed on this same set, raising overfitting concerns; no held-out benchmark or established negation benchmark (e.g., TIIF-Bench, NegBench-style data) is used.

The headline claim that VSF beats CFG 'even in non-few-step models' is confounded: VSF is applied to SD-3.5-Large-Turbo while CFG is applied to the non-distilled SD-3.5-Large, so model differences and guidance-scale choices are entangled with the guidance method.

Noticeable drop in positive prompt adherence for VSF (0.870 vs ~0.99 for baselines); while framed as a trade-off, the paper does not provide a principled way for users to select the operating point, and MLLM scores make the trade-off hard to interpret.

Poor polish undermines confidence: leftover artifacts such as 'ChatGPT said:' in Section 4.5, broken citations rendered as '?', typos ('REMOVEL', 'tunning', 'comparsion', 'Knoest', 'CaucVid'), and inconsistent equation notation (Eq. 1 uses xt+1 and xt−1 inconsistently).
Runtime claims are mixed: although theoretically cheaper than NAG/NASA, measured SD3.5 runtime is on par with NAG due to FlashAttention masking limitations, weakening the efficiency advantage claim.
No code release or reproducibility details for the MMDiT masking implementation, which is the crux of the method.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and practically important problem: negative prompt guidance is incompatible with step-distilled (few-step) models, where CFG degrades output quality and doubles runtime. The proposed VSF is simple, elegant, and nearly free of computational overhead.

The method is well-motivated: adaptively steering away from negative concepts proportional to the current image-to-negative attention strength, which improves upon the fixed-scale subtraction in NASA and the extrapolation-based NAG.

The experimental section is relatively broad: comparisons with NAG, NAG++, a reimplementation of NASA, CFG on non-distilled SD3.5, and external baselines (GPT-4o, Janus-4o, Qwen-Image, a generate-then-edit pipeline); plus hyperparameter trade-off sweeps, an ablation of masking/duplication/bias, a WEF negative-control experiment, attention map visualization, computational cost measurements, and adaptation to a video model (Wan 2.1 with CausVid LoRA).
The authors are candid about limitations, including MLLM judge unreliability, over-removal of semantically related features, and the failure on Flux Schnell.
weaknesses: Severe writing/polish problems that are unacceptable at a top venue: a leftover 'ChatGPT said:' appears verbatim in the Results section (Page 8), broken citations rendered as '(?)' appear twice (Pages 7 and 10), and numerous typos ('Flex Schnell', 'Knoest' for Kontext, 'PADDING REMOVEL', 'comparsion', 'tunning', 'disstilled'). These suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

The central claims rest on a single MLLM-as-judge metric (Llama 4 Maverick) over a self-generated set of only 200 prompts (2 seeds) created by ChatGPT o3, which the authors themselves acknowledge is error-prone and biased toward over-estimating quality. The claimed human evaluation between VSF and NAG is mentioned but no results are ever reported.

No standard image quality / preference metrics (ImageReward, HPSv2, etc.) are reported at all; the justification for omitting them is speculative. The quality advantage over baselines is therefore not convincingly established, particularly since VSF's positive score drops substantially (0.870 vs 0.990 for no guidance and 1.000 for CFG) and the qualitative examples show over-simplified or over-removed content.

Novelty is modest: VSF is essentially NASA's fixed-scale value subtraction made adaptive by concatenating negative keys/values into the softmax; the adaptivity idea is acknowledged to come from Koulischer et al. and Schramowski et al., and token-level modulation was already hypothesized in NAG's future work section.

The NASA baseline is a reimplementation by the authors (original code unavailable), and NAG's hyperparameters were manually re-tuned by the authors without a systematic sweep for the main results, raising fairness concerns about the baseline comparison.

Claims that VSF 'even outperforms CFG in non-few-step models' are overstated: the negative score is higher (0.545 vs 0.300) but at a large cost in positive adherence (0.870 vs 1.000), which the headline framing does not adequately convey.
Reproducibility details are thin: no code release is mentioned, the evaluation prompts/judges are custom and not standardized, and results on Wan are qualitative only in the appendix.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: negative prompt guidance for few-step distilled diffusion/flow-matching models (SD3.5 Turbo, Wan 2.1 with CausVid LoRA), where CFG is known to fail.

The core idea (Value Sign Flip) is simple and cheap: flipping the sign of negative-prompt values inside attention avoids double forward passes, unlike CFG, and the softmax structure naturally yields adaptive, token/layer/step-dependent guidance strength without extra machinery.
The MMDiT adaptation (token duplication, attention masking, attention bias, padding removal) is carefully reasoned and shows awareness of practical integration issues.

Evaluation is broader than typical: MLLM-as-judge quantitative results, McNemar significance tests, qualitative comparisons, a hyperparameter trade-off frontier analysis (Figure 8), an ablation including a simpler WEF baseline (Figure 9), external baselines (GPT-4o, Janus-4o, Qwen-Image, generate-then-edit), runtime/VRAM measurements (Table 3), and video results on Wan 2.1.
Honest discussion of limitations: over-removal of semantically related features, failures on abstract concepts, MLLM judge unreliability, and the method not helping Flux Schnell.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially NASA with an adaptive weighting induced by softmax, plus engineering fixes (masking/duplication). The paper itself positions VSF as drawing directly from NASA, NAG, Koulischer et al., and Schramowski et al.; the conceptual increment over NASA is thin.

Headline claims are stronger than the evidence: in Table 2, VSF's positive score (0.870) is markedly lower than all baselines (0.970-1.000) and its quality score is also lower than NAG; the main win is negative score only. The trade-off discussion does not fully resolve whether VSF dominates in a practically meaningful way.

Human evaluation is claimed ('we also did a human evaluation between our model and NAG for pairwise comparison') but no results are ever reported anywhere in the paper, leaving the subjective quality claim unsupported.

Evaluation depends entirely on a single MLLM judge (llama-4-maverick), which the authors themselves admit is unreliable for quality (Figure 6) and prone to hallucination; no alternative metrics (e.g., CLIP/NegCLIP-based negation scores) are provided. The dataset is only 200 o3-generated prompts x 2 seeds, with acknowledged repetition, raising concerns about coverage and generalization.

NASA baseline is a reimplementation based on NAG's codebase rather than official code, which weakens baseline fairness; hyperparameters for baselines were 'moderately and manually' re-tuned, another source of potential bias.

Serious writing/presentation problems that undermine confidence: leftover text 'ChatGPT said:' appears in Section 4.5; multiple typos ('REMOVEL', 'Abliation', 'Tunning', 'torward', 'releative', 'Flex Schnell', 'unbrulla', 'Comparsion'); Eq. (1) uses x_{t+1} and x_{t-1} inconsistently; citations render as '(?)' for the LLaMA judge and MMMU scores; 'von Platen et al.' lacks a year.
No statement of code release, limiting reproducibility; the video evaluation is purely qualitative in the appendix with no quantitative negative-score comparison for Wan.

The 'adaptive' advantage over prior fixed-scale methods is asserted but not rigorously analyzed (e.g., no direct comparison against the probability-based dynamic scaling of Koulischer et al. 2025a, which is the most natural adaptive baseline).

strengths: Addresses a real and practically important problem: negative prompt guidance in few-step (1-8 step) distilled diffusion/flow-matching models where standard CFG fails or is unusable.

The core mechanism is elegant and well-motivated: sign-flipping negative prompt values within attention is shown (with a proof in the appendix) to be exactly equivalent to token-weighted adaptive subtraction (Eq. 7-8), giving a dynamic, token/layer/step-adaptive guidance weight at essentially single-pass cost.

Careful engineering for MMDiT-style models: the duplication + attention-masking design (N^(0) unflipped collector path, N^(1) flipped and only attended by image tokens, bias -beta) is well reasoned, with ablations isolating each component (WEF baseline, no-mask, no-bias variants).

Broad empirical coverage: SD3.5-Large-Turbo, Flux Schnell, and Wan video; comparisons against NAG, NAG Strong (re-tuned), NASA, vanilla CFG, and external pipelines (generate-then-edit, GPT-4o, Nano Banana, Janus-4o, Qwen-Image); ablations on alpha/beta; trade-off sweeps (66 VSF vs 287 NAG runs); runtime/VRAM analysis.

Contributions beyond the method: a new challenging benchmark (NegGenBench) with intentionally coupled negative prompts, a fine-tuned negation-aware evaluator (NegAwareQwen), and honest discussion of evaluator limitations, failure cases, and human-validation agreement.

Results are convincing in relative terms: VSF achieves substantially higher negative scores than NAG/NASA at comparable or better quality, and even beats CFG in non-few-step models on negative adherence; human validation and the fine-tuned evaluator qualitatively agree with the LLaMA-based ranking.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on MLLM-as-judge evaluation (LLaMA-4 Maverick) whose reliability the authors themselves show is limited: human-MLLM quality correlation is weak (R^2=0.336 for log fit), MLLM overestimates quality, and different MLLM providers were used for different portions of the experiment, adding metric instability.

Human validation is very small: only 10 prompts x 2 seeds (20 images per method), so Table 3 differences (e.g., negative score 0.55 vs 0.25) carry large uncertainty; the main benchmark is also modest (200 prompts, 2 seeds, single generation seed for much of the sweep).

Novelty is moderate/incremental: the method is an explicit extension of NASA, Koulischer et al.'s dynamic guidance, and Schramowski et al., and NAG's future work already hinted at token-level modulation; the conceptual step from attention-output subtraction to value sign-flipping is neat but narrow.
NASA baseline was reimplemented on NAG's codebase because official code was unavailable, introducing potential implementation-fairness concerns for a key comparison.

The benchmark prompts/negative pairs are generated by ChatGPT and evaluation questions are also LLM-generated, which risks benchmark bias toward methods (and evaluators) that follow the same style of negation phrasing.

Some headline framing overstates evidence: 'even CFG in non-few-step models' is shown only on their own self-defined benchmark with an LLM judge; and the 'Generate+Edit' style baseline's negative score (0.488) is close to VSF Quality (0.420) at lower quality, complicating the 'best in open source' claim depending on operating point.

Several important details (exact metrics prompts, sweep protocol restricted to first 100 prompts, GPU thermal-throttling protocol) introduce reproducibility caveats, and code/dataset are only promised post-publication.

strengths: Addresses a real and practically important problem: negative prompt guidance is incompatible with or degrades few-step distilled models (CFG fails, NAG/NASA have limitations), so a cheap single-pass alternative is valuable to practitioners.

The core idea (flipping the sign of negative-prompt attention values) is elegant and well-motivated, and the paper honestly proves it is mathematically equivalent to token-weighted subtraction (Appendix B), which clarifies its relationship to NASA.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: SD3.5 Turbo, Flux Schnell, and Wan video models; comparisons against NAG, NASA, CFG, and external baselines (GPT-4o, Nano Banana, generate-then-edit); computational cost analysis (Table 6); attention-map visualization; and trade-off sweeps (66/287/10 runs).

Includes ablation studies (WEF, masking, bias, duplication), hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, a modest human validation, and a secondary evaluation with a fine-tuned negation-aware evaluator (NegAwareQwen), which partially mitigates single-judge concerns.
Introduction of the NegGenBench dataset with challenging positive-negative prompt pairs is a useful community resource, and the paper is transparent about MLLM-as-judge limitations.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially NASA with an adaptive, attention-ratio-derived per-token weight, explicitly extending Koulischer et al. (2025) and Schramowski et al. (2023) to token level in few-step models; the authors themselves acknowledge this lineage, and the equivalent formulation (Eq. 7) shows the contribution is a fairly direct combination of prior ideas.

Evaluation reliability is a significant concern: the primary metric is LLaMA-4-Maverick as judge, with the authors' own reported F1 of only 0.667 for negative-score agreement with humans, and acknowledged MLLM quality overestimation (Figure 11). Human validation covers only 10 prompts x 2 seeds, which is far too small to substantiate headline claims.

The fine-tuned evaluator (NegAwareQwen) is trained on data generated by the authors' own methods (VSF, NAG, NASA) with their own scoring labels, introducing potential circularity/bias favoring their approach; it is also presented as 'future work' resource rather than a validated benchmark.

The benchmark is small and synthetic: 200 prompts generated by ChatGPT o3 with only 2 seeds for main results, and the sweep evaluations use only the first 100 prompts with a single seed; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are provided anywhere.

Inconsistencies and reproducibility gaps: results differ between evaluators (e.g., VSF Quality negative score 0.420 vs 0.330 in Table 8), different MLLM providers were used for different experiment portions (acknowledged), NASA is a re-implementation rather than official code, and code/dataset are only promised 'after publication.'

Writing quality is below the bar for a top venue: numerous typos ('unbrulla', 'Abliation', 'Comparsion', 'promtes', 'Flex Schnell', 'negotiation-aware' for negation-aware), Eq. 1 appears to contain a typo (xt+1 vs xt-1), and Figure 2 caption/formatting issues; the abstract's claim of being 'a suppressed generate-then-edit pipeline' is unclear.

Some central claims are weaker than the evidence: the 'even beats CFG' claim compares few-step VSF against CFG on a 28-step model where the operating points and runtimes differ substantially, and the style-avoidance/anti-aesthetics applications are anecdotal (a handful of qualitative examples).

strengths: Addresses a clear, practically important problem: negative prompt guidance in few-step distilled diffusion/flow models where CFG fails or doubles runtime

The core idea (flipping the sign of negative-prompt attention values within the attention computation) is simple, elegant, and well-motivated as a dynamic, token/layer/step-adaptive form of negative guidance, with a clean equivalence proof to token-weighted subtraction

Thoughtful engineering for MMDiT-style architectures (negative prompt duplication, attention masking, attention bias, padding removal), plus demonstrations on cross-attention models (Wan video, Flux Schnell)

Fairly comprehensive evaluation: comparisons to NAG, NAG Strong (re-tuned), NASA, CFG, and external baselines including GPT-4o, Nano Banana, generate-then-edit; trade-off curves via hyperparameter sweeps; ablation study including the informative negative result that whole-embedding flip (WEF) does not work
Effort to make evaluation more trustworthy: human validation, a fine-tuned negation-aware evaluator (NegAwareQwen), attention map visualizations, failure cases, and computational cost analysis
Releases a new challenging benchmark (NegGenBench) and promises code, ComfyUI node, and dataset
weaknesses: Evaluation is built entirely on a small self-constructed benchmark (200 prompts, 2 seeds) with prompts generated by ChatGPT o3; risk of benchmark design bias toward the proposed method, and no comparison to existing negation benchmarks

Primary evaluation uses an MLLM judge whose reliability is questionable: reported F1 of 0.667 for negative score vs. human labels is only moderate; human validation covers only 10 prompts (20 images), so cross-validation evidence is thin

Potential hyperparameter overfitting: VSF hyperparameters and NAG Strong settings are tuned on the same prompt set used for final evaluation; the sweep for trade-off curves uses only the first 100 prompts with a single seed
NASA baseline is a re-implementation (no official code), raising fairness concerns in that comparison; NAG Strong hyperparameters are manually re-tuned by the authors
Absolute negative scores remain low (0.42-0.545), and the semantic gap between 'best' and 'decent' (e.g., vs. Nano Banana at 0.498) is not statistically tested; no variance/significance reporting
Writing quality issues: multiple typos ('unbrulla', 'abliation', 'torward', 'Comparsion'), unclear sentences (e.g., 'Our method is also a suppressed generate-then-edit pipeline'), which reduce polish

No theoretical or empirical analysis of failure modes related to the method itself (e.g., when the negative concept is entangled with the subject, as in the house-roof failure), only anecdotal failure examples
Code/dataset not yet available at review time, limiting verifiability of the re-implementations and evaluation pipeline
